findings.assertion: The military capitulation of Mexico City on 21 June 1867 and Juárez's ceremonial return on 15 July were distinct events. A telegram sent by Porfirio Díaz from Tacubaya to the minister of war reports surrender of the capital's defenders and asks that the republican government return; later ceremony narratives date the public entry to 15 July.
findings.source_locator: Díaz edited telegram HTML lines 11–15; Tovar/Mas historical account lines 54–61
findings.limitations: No original telegram or military capitulation instrument inspected; 21 June seizure must not be collapsed into 15 July civilian reception.

findings.assertion: Juárez's 15 July 1867 manifesto claims legal continuity of constitutional government during four years away from the capital; it explicitly links the government's return to the 1857 constitutional order and distinguishes national sovereignty from the geography of where ministers resided.
findings.source_locator: UNAM edited primary manifesto pp.456–457 (PDF pages 1–2), page images verified
findings.limitations: This is the government's self-description in a partisan state document, not an independent adjudication of full legal continuity. UNAM adapted spelling from Dublán and Lozano (1878).

findings.assertion: The manifesto asks inhabitants to respect laws, balance leniency with necessary justice for former opponents, and resume elections after extraordinary wartime powers; a claim that the ceremony instantly restored ordinary democratic practice would overstate the document.
findings.source_locator: UNAM manifesto p.457; Carmona edited transcript HTML lines 24–29
findings.limitations: Original election call, voting rules, implementation and opponents' responses remain unexamined; aspirational language cannot stand in for actual electoral outcomes.

findings.assertion: During the Maximilian government, the Zócalo was planted and equipped as a public promenade in 1866: the INAH archaeological history describes crossing walks, corner fountains, 62 iron benches, trees and gas illumination. Juárez's 1867 entry therefore took place on a square already altered under the empire.
findings.source_locator: INAH Boletín no.46, p.123 text and screenshot, note 69
findings.limitations: Published study cites Jesús Galindo y Villa for 1866 equipment; municipal invoices/period visual confirmation absent. Gas lighting is an 1866 historic claim, not current feature.

findings.assertion: The public celebrations combined arches, laurel honors, public decoration, military displays and speeches; published historical reconstructions differ about the Alameda banquet, noting a storm and an indoor reception at the Colegio de Minas. The route and banquets must not be flattened into a single uninterrupted street event.
findings.source_locator: Tovar/Mas HTML lines 57–83; Carmona HTML lines 15–19
findings.limitations: Original 15–16 July El Siglo Diez y Nueve and El Globo issues not read; ceremonial timing and banquet location require document-by-document comparison.

findings.assertion: A historically described entry sequence crosses the Chapultepec approach and Puerta de Belén, proceeds via Bucareli, passes the old Carlos IV statue near Reforma/Bucareli and continues along the former street network to today's Avenida Juárez/Madero before reaching the Plaza. A guide can teach street-name change without claiming a verified turn-by-turn 1867 GPS alignment.
findings.limitations: Historic maps and gate locations not georeferenced. The monument 'El Caballito' subsequently relocated; do not direct visitor to assume original 1867 statue location remains.

findings.assertion: At the 1867 festivities a temporary allegorical Victory sculpture occupied the unfinished 1843 Independence Monument pedestal in the Zócalo. The INAH study identifies the sculpture as starting to be removed on 5 September 1867 after cracking and shedding pieces, citing 6 and 8 September contemporary press accounts.
findings.source_locator: INAH Boletín no.46 p.123, notes 70–72 (Boletín Republicano 1867-06-17 p2; El Siglo Diez y Nueve 1867-09-06 p3; Boletín Republicano 1867-09-08 p3); Tovar/Mas lines 30–32
findings.limitations: Original newspapers not directly examined and 1867 photo reproduction rights not cleared; no extant Victory statue is visible today.

findings.assertion: The Zócalo's popular name derives from the unfinished 1843 monument foundation, not from the 1910 Angel on Paseo de la Reforma. INAH reports that the original foundation persists beneath plaza paving; in 2017 workers encountered circular platform and banqueta elements north of the central flagpole and protected them again after documentation.
findings.source_locator: INAH Boletín no.46 pp.112–114, 118, 129; p.129 inscribed plaque wording and coverings
findings.limitations: Modern plaques and visibility have NOT been physically verified in 2026; a hidden foundation must not be described as an open excavated ruin.

findings.assertion: François Aubert's 1867 image of Juárez's entry at Palacio Nacional has a cited INAH-Sinafo inventory number (the historical essay uses 181419; an INAH paper figure labels a separate reproduced Aubert image inv. 628364). These catalog numbers must not be equated or images reused without license clearance.
findings.source_locator: Tovar/Mas HTML line 32; INAH Boletín no.46 fig.16 p.123 photo caption inv.628364
findings.limitations: Photo title, negative, positive, inventory equivalence and image-use permission not independently verified; feature candidate only.

findings.assertion: The uncompleted 1843 foundation engineering used timber piles and crossed cedar beam-grillages beneath masonry. The INAH archaeological paper compares its 2017 section to nineteenth-century engineering reports, including a reported 1,927 cedar stakes (historic record) and measurements of a smaller archaeological sample; do not misrepresent all reported dimensions as measured in situ.
findings.source_locator: INAH Boletín no.46 pp.115–117, fig.11 and notes 33–42
findings.limitations: Published dimensions mix 1840s reported quantities with 2017 sample observations; original engineering reports and full excavation archive not independently read.

findings.assertion: The buried monument remains were encountered in separate campaigns: a 1983 test for a cancelled Line 8 Metro proposal and 2017 Zócalo rehabilitation. The archaeologists distinguish a 35 m base ring, an 8 m later platform, and a 14 m circular banqueta, partly affected by 1999 flagpole foundations; these phases are later than the Mexica sacred precinct.
findings.source_locator: INAH Boletín no.46 pp.112–115,118,129, fig.8; preliminary historic precinct bounds p.108
findings.limitations: Original 1983 Miranda report and 2017 final DSA dossier not examined; printed figures do not establish 2026 exposure or exact field access. Do not equate this monument base with Templo Mayor structure.
